newsitem.title: INDIA: Kazakh plane "black boxes" found after crash.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh plane "black boxes" found after crash.

text.p: Searchers have found the first "black boxes" that might explain why two planes collided in mid-air near New Delhi, killing some 350 people, an airline official said on Wednesday.
Rajiv Bhaskar told Reuters the flight data and cockpit voice recorders of the Kazakh Airlines cargo plane which collided in mid-air with a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet had been found.

Bhaskar, the Delhi airport manager of Kazakh Airlines, said the so-called "black boxes" were found in the wreckage of the Ilyushin Il-76 after the world's worst mid-air collision on Tuesday evening 80 km (50 miles) from the Indian capital.
He said the plane was carrying 27 passengers, including two children, and 10 crew members.
Officials in Almaty, the Kazhak capital, had said earlier the plane was carrying 39 people.
There were 312 people aboard the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747.
Passengers aboard the Kazakh plane were businessmen who had chartered it for the flight to New Delhi, where they had planned to buy Indian goods and fly them back home, Bhaskar said.
He said businessmen chartered planes from Almaty regularly for buying trips to India.
They intended to buy wool items, which are cheap in India, to sell them back home where the weather is getting colder.
Search teams had retrieved all 37 bodies from the Kazakh plane, which crashed in flames some 10 km (six miles) from where the Saudi Boeing 747 plunged to earth, Bhaskar said.

He said Indian civil aviation officials, who were at the Saudi plane crash site, had not yet inspected the debris of the Kazakh aircraft and the data recorders had been put under guard until they arrived to take them away.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was due to visit the sites on Wednesday.
The Saudi jumbo also crashed in a fireball after taking off from Delhi with a full load of fuel. Charred and mangled bodies were strewn throughout the debris over a wide area.
The Press Trust of India said search teams found two completely intact bodies -- a mother and child clinging to each other.
Why the planes collided is not known. But experts offered several likely reasons, including possibly inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport, language difficulties and pilot error.
Some said many pilots from the former Soviet Union often had difficulty understanding English, the language of international aviation.
Bhaskar said that was an unlikely explanation.
"If that was the case we would have accidents every other day," he said. "I believe the cause of the collision was either pilot error or control tower error."
He did not comment on suggestions that the pilot of the Kazazh freighter might have miscalculated the conversion into metres of control tower instructions given in feet.
The Saudi plane was told to climb to 14,000 feet (4,308 metres) after taking off for Dhahran and Jeddah.
The Kazakh aircraft, which was coming into land on the same flight corridor, was instructed to maintain a height of 15,000 feet (4,615 metres), Indian aviation officials said.
Experts said altimeters in aircraft in the former Soviet Union were calibrated in metres, unlike most planes elsewhere which were in feet.
Unless the Kazakh aircraft had an altimeter that expressed its height in both measurements, the pilot could have made a mistake in the conversion, they said.
